topics.title: Business Cycles & Economic Indicators
topics.reading:
The business cycle

Economies do not grow in a straight line. They move through a recurring pattern of rising and falling activity called the business cycle. The four phases, in order, are:

  1. Expansion – rising GDP, employment, consumer spending, industrial production and (usually) stock prices. Late in an expansion, demand can outrun supply and inflation begins to rise.
  2. Peak – the high point of activity. Capacity is stretched, inflation pressure and interest rates are typically elevated.
  3. Contraction – GDP falls, unemployment rises, inventories build up, and corporate profits decline. A contraction is popularly called a recession when real GDP declines for two consecutive quarters; a depression is a severe, prolonged decline (the traditional test answer is six consecutive quarters).
  4. Trough – the low point, after which recovery (a new expansion) begins.
Exam tip: Remember the order "expansion, peak, contraction, trough." A question asking what comes immediately after a trough wants "expansion" (recovery). In the U.S., the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) officially dates recessions, but the two-quarter rule is the exam's shorthand.

Different industries respond differently to the cycle. Cyclical industries (autos, heavy equipment, housing, luxury goods, travel) rise and fall sharply with the economy. Defensive industries (food, utilities, pharmaceuticals, tobacco, basic household products) hold up relatively well in recessions because people keep buying necessities. Growth industries grow faster than the overall economy regardless of the cycle. Countercyclical businesses (e.g., discount retailers, debt collectors) may actually do better when the economy weakens.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP)

GDP is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a period. It is the broadest measure of economic output. Using the expenditure approach: GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government spending + (Exports − Imports). Consumer spending is the largest component of U.S. GDP (roughly two-thirds). Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation (using the GDP deflator), so real GDP is the figure used to judge whether the economy actually grew.

Leading, coincident and lagging indicators

Economists group data by when it tends to move relative to the overall cycle.

TypeTimingExamples
LeadingChanges before the economy turns; used to forecastBuilding permits (new private housing), average weekly hours of manufacturing workers, new orders for consumer goods and capital goods, initial weekly unemployment claims, S&P 500 stock prices, money supply (M2—a traditional textbook leading indicator, though the Conference Board replaced it with a leading credit index in 2012), yield spread (10-year Treasury minus fed funds), consumer expectations
CoincidentMoves with the economy; confirms the current phaseNonfarm payroll employment, personal income (less transfer payments), industrial production, manufacturing and trade sales
LaggingChanges after the economy turns; confirms a trendAverage duration of unemployment, change in the CPI for services, average prime rate charged by banks, commercial and industrial loans outstanding, consumer credit to personal income ratio, labor cost per unit of output, inventories-to-sales ratio
Trap: Stock prices are a leading indicator—markets anticipate the economy. Building permits lead because they come before construction activity. "Duration of unemployment," "prime rate" and "CPI for services" are lagging. Industrial production and nonfarm payrolls are coincident. Initial jobless claims are leading, but the average duration of unemployment is lagging—don't confuse the two employment measures.

Employment and prices

The unemployment rate (from the Bureau of Labor Statistics) is the percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unemployed. Employment reports are closely watched because payroll growth drives consumer spending. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures changes in the prices of a basket of goods and services purchased by urban consumers and is the most widely cited measure of inflation; core CPI excludes volatile food and energy prices. The Producer Price Index (PPI) tracks wholesale/producer prices and is sometimes viewed as an early signal of consumer inflation.

Trade deficit and balance of payments

A trade deficit exists when a country imports more goods and services than it exports; a trade surplus is the reverse. The balance of payments records all transactions between a country and the rest of the world. Its current account includes trade in goods and services, investment income and transfers; its capital/financial account records purchases and sales of assets (e.g., foreigners buying U.S. Treasuries or U.S. firms building plants abroad). A current account deficit is financed by a capital/financial account surplus—foreign investment flowing into the country.
keyPoints: Business cycle order: expansion, peak, contraction, trough, then expansion again.
Exam rule of thumb: recession = two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP; depression = severe, prolonged decline (six quarters).
GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); real GDP is adjusted for inflation; consumer spending is the largest component.
Leading indicators: building permits, stock prices, new orders, average weekly hours, initial jobless claims, yield spread (textbooks also list money supply/M2).
Coincident: nonfarm payrolls, personal income, industrial production, manufacturing and trade sales.
Lagging: duration of unemployment, prime rate, CPI for services, loans outstanding, labor cost per unit.
Defensive industries (food, utilities, drugs) hold up in recessions; cyclical industries (autos, housing, durable goods) swing with the economy.
Trade deficit = imports exceed exports; balance of payments = current account + capital/financial account.

topics.title: Monetary & Fiscal Policy
topics.reading:
Two levers on the economy

Governments try to smooth the business cycle—promoting maximum employment and stable prices—with two sets of tools. Monetary policy is controlled by the Federal Reserve (the Fed) and works through the money supply and interest rates. Fiscal policy is controlled by Congress and the President and works through government spending and taxation.

Exam tip: If the question mentions taxes, government spending, budgets or deficits, it's fiscal policy (Congress/President). If it mentions the money supply, reserves, the discount rate or open market operations, it's monetary policy (the Fed). The Fed cannot change tax rates.

The Federal Reserve's tools

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) directs monetary policy. The Fed's tools:

  • Open market operations – the Fed buys or sells U.S. government securities (mainly Treasuries) in the open market. This is the most frequently used and most flexible tool. When the Fed buys securities, it pays with newly created bank reserves, increasing the money supply and pushing rates down (easing). When the Fed sells securities, it drains reserves, decreasing the money supply and pushing rates up (tightening).
  • Discount rate – the rate the Fed charges member banks that borrow directly from it at the "discount window." It is the one rate the Fed sets directly. Raising it discourages bank borrowing (tight); lowering it encourages borrowing (easy).
  • Reserve requirements – the percentage of deposits banks must hold in reserve rather than lend. Raising the requirement shrinks lending capacity (tight); lowering it expands lending (easy). It is considered the most powerful but least used tool because small changes have large effects through the money multiplier. (Since March 2020 the Fed has set reserve requirements at 0%, but the exam still tests the concept.)
  • Interest on reserve balances – in practice the Fed now also steers short-term rates by setting the interest it pays banks on reserves; raising it encourages banks to hold rather than lend money.
  • Moral suasion – the Fed's public statements ("jawboning") and forward guidance influence expectations.

The federal funds rate and other short-term rates

The federal funds rate is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves. The FOMC sets a target range and uses its tools to keep the market rate within it; it is the most sensitive indicator of Fed policy and of the direction of short-term rates. Other rates to know: the prime rate is what banks charge their most creditworthy corporate customers (set by banks, tends to follow fed funds); the broker call loan rate is what banks charge broker-dealers for loans used to finance customer margin accounts.

GoalOpen market opsDiscount rateReserve req.Money supply / rates
Ease (stimulate)Fed buys securitiesLowerLowerMoney supply up, rates down
Tighten (fight inflation)Fed sells securitiesRaiseRaiseMoney supply down, rates up
Trap: "The Fed sets the federal funds rate" is not quite right—the Fed sets a target for it; banks set the actual rate among themselves. The Fed directly sets the discount rate. The prime rate is set by commercial banks.

Fiscal policy

Expansionary fiscal policy means increasing government spending and/or cutting taxes—both put more money in the economy and stimulate demand, but they tend to increase budget deficits. Contractionary fiscal policy means reducing spending and/or raising taxes to cool an overheating economy. Keynesian economists emphasize an active role for government spending (fiscal policy) to manage demand. Monetarists (associated with Milton Friedman) believe the money supply is the key driver of economic activity and inflation. Supply-side economists emphasize lower tax rates to encourage production and investment.

Effects on markets

Easy money generally lowers interest rates, raises bond prices and supports stock prices; tight money raises rates, lowers bond prices and tends to pressure stocks. Rising deficits financed by more Treasury borrowing can push interest rates up (the "crowding out" effect on private borrowers).
keyPoints: Monetary policy = the Federal Reserve (FOMC); fiscal policy = Congress and the President (taxes and spending).
Open market operations are the most frequently used, most flexible Fed tool; Fed buying = easing, Fed selling = tightening.
Discount rate = rate the Fed charges member banks; it is the rate the Fed directly sets.
Reserve requirement = most powerful, least used tool; lower requirement expands lending.
Fed funds rate = overnight bank-to-bank lending rate; FOMC sets a target; most sensitive indicator of rate direction.
Prime rate = rate banks charge best corporate customers; broker call rate = rate banks charge broker-dealers for margin loans.
Expansionary fiscal policy = more spending and/or lower taxes; contractionary = less spending and/or higher taxes.
Monetarists focus on money supply; Keynesians focus on government spending/aggregate demand; supply-siders focus on lower tax rates.

topics.title: Inflation, Interest Rates, Yield Curves & Credit Spreads
topics.reading:
Inflation and deflation

Inflation is a persistent rise in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money. Demand-pull inflation occurs when too much money chases too few goods (strong demand); cost-push inflation occurs when rising input costs (wages, energy) push prices up. Moderate inflation (the Fed targets about 2%) is normal in a growing economy. Deflation is a persistent decline in prices; it usually accompanies weak demand and can be dangerous because consumers postpone purchases and the real burden of debt rises. Disinflation is a slowing of the rate of inflation (prices still rising, just more slowly). Stagflation combines high inflation with stagnant growth and high unemployment.

Who is hurt by inflation? Holders of fixed-income investments (bonds, fixed annuities, CDs) and people on fixed incomes. Who benefits? Borrowers repaying debt with cheaper dollars, and owners of real assets (real estate, commodities) that tend to rise with prices. Common stocks have historically been the best long-term hedge against inflation; TIPS provide an explicit hedge.

Nominal vs. real interest rates

The nominal rate is the stated rate. The real rate adjusts for inflation:

Real rate of return ≈ nominal return − inflation rate

Example: a bond fund returns 6% in a year when the CPI rises 2.5%. Real return ≈ 6% − 2.5% = 3.5%. If a 3% CD is held while inflation runs 4%, the real return is −1%—purchasing power fell even though the account balance grew. For an inflation-adjusted after-tax return, first take taxes out of the nominal return, then subtract inflation: a 5% taxable yield for an investor in the 24% bracket is 3.8% after tax; with 3% inflation the real after-tax return is 0.8%.

Interest rates and bond prices

Bond prices and interest rates move inversely. When market rates rise, existing bonds with lower coupons fall in price; when rates fall, existing bonds rise. Longer maturities and lower coupons mean greater price sensitivity (duration).

The yield curve

The yield curve plots yields of bonds of the same credit quality (usually Treasuries) against time to maturity.

  • Normal (positive, ascending) – long-term yields are higher than short-term yields. This is the usual shape, reflecting compensation for the added risk of lending longer (liquidity preference) and expectations of steady growth.
  • Inverted (negative, descending) – short-term yields exceed long-term yields. It usually occurs when the Fed has tightened aggressively and investors expect rates to fall in the future; historically an inverted curve has been a reliable signal of a coming recession.
  • Flat – short and long yields are about the same; often a transition between normal and inverted.
  • Humped – intermediate yields are highest.

Theories explaining the shape: the expectations theory (the curve reflects expected future short-term rates), the liquidity preference theory (investors demand a premium to tie up money longer, so the normal curve slopes upward), and the market segmentation theory (supply and demand in separate maturity segments set yields).

Exam tip: Rising short-term rates with steady or falling long-term rates = the curve is flattening toward inversion. If an investor expects rates to fall, lock in long-term yields (and long bonds will gain the most in price).

Credit (yield) spreads

The credit spread is the difference in yield between a riskier bond (e.g., a corporate or high-yield bond) and a Treasury of the same maturity. Spreads reflect perceived default risk:

  • Widening spreads – investors demand more compensation for credit risk; typically a sign of economic worry or an approaching recession ("flight to quality" into Treasuries).
  • Narrowing spreads – investors are confident; typical of economic expansion.
Trap: A widening spread between high-yield and Treasury bonds is a negative sign for the economy, not a bullish one. And an inverted yield curve is a warning of recession, not of inflation getting out of control.
keyPoints: Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation; after-tax real return: take out taxes first, then subtract inflation.
Inflation hurts fixed-income holders and lenders; helps borrowers and owners of real assets.
Deflation = falling prices; disinflation = slower inflation; stagflation = high inflation + stagnant growth/high unemployment.
Bond prices move inversely to interest rates; long maturities and low coupons are most sensitive.
Normal yield curve slopes upward; inverted (short > long) historically signals recession; flat is transitional.
Theories: expectations, liquidity preference (explains upward slope), market segmentation.
Widening credit spreads = rising fear/recession risk; narrowing spreads = confidence/expansion.

topics.title: Global & Geopolitical Factors: Currencies & Sovereign Debt
topics.reading:
Exchange rates

An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. Most major currencies, including the U.S. dollar, float—their values are set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market. Factors that tend to strengthen a currency include higher relative interest rates (attracting foreign capital), lower inflation, a strong economy and political stability. Factors that weaken it include low interest rates, high inflation, large deficits and political turmoil.

Strong dollar vs. weak dollar

SituationWho benefitsWho is hurt
Strong (rising) dollar – each dollar buys more foreign currencyU.S. importers; U.S. consumers buying imported goods; Americans traveling abroad; foreign exporters selling to the U.S.U.S. exporters (their goods cost more overseas); U.S. multinationals translating foreign profits back into dollars; U.S. investors holding foreign-currency assets
Weak (falling) dollar – each dollar buys less foreign currencyU.S. exporters; U.S. multinationals with large foreign sales; U.S. investors holding foreign-currency assets; the U.S. tourism industryU.S. importers and consumers of imported goods; Americans traveling abroad

A weak dollar also tends to narrow a trade deficit over time, because U.S. exports become cheaper for foreigners while imports become more expensive for Americans.

Currency and foreign investing

When a U.S. investor buys a foreign stock or bond, the return in dollars depends on both the local-market return and the change in the exchange rate. Example: a U.S. investor buys a European stock that rises 8% in euros during the year. If the euro rises 5% against the dollar, the investor's dollar return is roughly 13%. If instead the euro falls 5%, the dollar return is only about 3%. This is exchange-rate (currency) risk. American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) trade in dollars but do not eliminate currency risk, since the underlying shares are valued in the foreign currency.

Exam tip: A U.S. investor who owns foreign securities is helped when the dollar weakens (the foreign currency buys more dollars when converted back). A U.S. investor planning a future purchase of foreign goods or securities is hurt by a weakening dollar.

Interest rates and currency

If U.S. interest rates rise relative to other countries, foreign investors buy dollar-denominated assets, increasing demand for dollars—so the dollar tends to strengthen. Conversely, a Fed easing cycle tends to weaken the dollar.

Sovereign debt

Sovereign debt is debt issued by a national government. Bonds issued by a stable government in its own currency (such as U.S. Treasuries) carry very low default risk because the government can tax and, ultimately, create money to pay. Sovereign bonds issued in a foreign currency (for example, an emerging-market country borrowing in U.S. dollars) carry more risk: if the local currency collapses, repaying dollar-denominated debt becomes much harder, and defaults have occurred (for example, Argentina's 2001 default on foreign-currency bonds). Credit rating agencies rate sovereign debt just as they rate corporate debt. High or rising sovereign debt can pressure a country's currency and raise its borrowing costs.

Geopolitical risk

Wars, trade disputes and tariffs, sanctions, elections, expropriation (nationalization of private assets) and changes in capital controls can affect markets, especially emerging markets. Political risk is the risk that government actions or instability in a country reduce the value of investments there. Emerging markets generally carry higher political, currency and liquidity risk than developed markets—along with higher potential return.

Trap: Currency risk exists even when a foreign security is bought in dollars (ADRs, global mutual funds). The investor's dollar return still depends on the foreign currency's movement.
keyPoints: Strong dollar helps U.S. importers and Americans traveling abroad; hurts U.S. exporters and U.S. holders of foreign assets.
Weak dollar helps U.S. exporters, multinationals and U.S. holders of foreign securities; hurts importers and U.S. travelers abroad.
Dollar return on a foreign investment ≈ local return + change in the foreign currency's value versus the dollar.
Higher relative U.S. interest rates attract foreign capital and tend to strengthen the dollar.
ADRs trade in dollars but still carry currency risk.
Sovereign debt = government debt; foreign-currency sovereign debt is riskier than debt in the issuer's own currency.
Political risk (expropriation, instability, sanctions) is greatest in emerging markets.

topics.title: Financial Statements: Balance Sheet, Income Statement & Cash Flows
topics.reading:
Why statements matter

Fundamental analysis evaluates a company's financial health and value using its financial statements, management, industry and the economy. The three core statements are the balance sheet, the income statement and the statement of cash flows, plus the footnotes that explain them.

The balance sheet (statement of financial condition)

The balance sheet is a snapshot at a single point in time. Its equation:

Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' (stockholders') equity, so Equity (net worth) = Assets − Liabilities.

  • Current assets – cash and equivalents, marketable securities, accounts receivable, inventory, prepaid expenses (expected to become cash within one year).
  • Fixed assets – property, plant and equipment, shown net of accumulated depreciation.
  • Intangible assets – goodwill, patents, trademarks.
  • Current liabilities – accounts payable, accrued wages and taxes, short-term notes, the current portion of long-term debt (due within one year).
  • Long-term liabilities – bonds and other debt due in more than one year.
  • Shareholders' equity – preferred stock, common stock at par, additional paid-in capital (capital surplus), retained earnings, minus treasury stock.

Working capital = current assets − current liabilities. It measures liquidity—the ability to meet short-term obligations. Book value per share = (total equity − preferred stock) ÷ common shares outstanding.

The income statement (profit and loss)

The income statement covers a period of time (a quarter or year). A simplified layout:

LineExample ($ millions)
Net sales (revenue)500
− Cost of goods sold(300)
= Gross profit200
− Operating expenses (SG&A, depreciation)(100)
= Operating income (EBIT)100
− Interest expense(20)
= Pretax income80
− Taxes (25%)(20)
= Net income60
− Preferred dividends(10)
= Earnings available to common50

EPS = (net income − preferred dividends) ÷ common shares outstanding. With 25 million shares, EPS = $50M ÷ 25M = $2.00. Note that bond interest is paid before taxes (it is deductible), while dividends are paid from after-tax income. Retained earnings grow by net income minus all dividends paid.

The statement of cash flows

Accounting profit is not the same as cash. The cash flow statement shows actual cash moving in and out, in three sections:

  • Operating activities – cash from the core business: net income adjusted for non-cash items (depreciation and amortization are added back) and changes in working capital.
  • Investing activities – buying or selling property, equipment, other businesses or investment securities (capital expenditures appear here).
  • Financing activities – issuing or repurchasing stock, issuing or repaying debt, and paying dividends.
Exam tip: Depreciation reduces reported earnings (and taxes) but uses no cash, so it is added back in operating cash flow. Paying a dividend is a financing outflow; buying a new factory is an investing outflow.
Trap: The balance sheet is "as of" one date; the income statement and cash flow statement cover "for the period ended." A question asking which statement shows a company's financial position at a moment in time wants the balance sheet.

Footnotes

Footnotes disclose accounting methods (e.g., inventory valuation such as FIFO vs. LIFO, depreciation methods), pending litigation, off-balance-sheet obligations and other details. Analysts consider them an essential part of the statements.
keyPoints: Balance sheet = snapshot at one point in time: Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' equity.
Income statement and cash flow statement cover a period of time.
Working capital = current assets − current liabilities (a liquidity measure).
EPS = (net income − preferred dividends) ÷ common shares outstanding.
Interest expense is paid before taxes; dividends are paid from after-tax net income.
Cash flow sections: operating (depreciation added back), investing (capex), financing (stock, debt, dividends).
Book value per share = (equity − preferred) ÷ common shares outstanding.
Footnotes disclose accounting methods, litigation and off-balance-sheet items.

topics.title: SEC Filings, Audits & Accounting Methods
topics.reading:
Periodic reporting under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934

Public companies (reporting issuers) must file regular reports with the SEC, available to the public through the EDGAR database. The three you must know:

FormWhat it isAudited?
10-KAnnual report: full audited financial statements, management's discussion and analysis (MD&A), risk factors, business description, executive compensation disclosures. Due 60–90 days after fiscal year-end depending on company size.Yes – financial statements audited by an independent public accountant
10-QQuarterly report filed for each of the first three fiscal quarters (no 10-Q for the fourth quarter; the 10-K covers it). Due 40–45 days after quarter-end.No – unaudited (reviewed, not audited)
8-K"Current report" disclosing material unscheduled events: a merger or acquisition, bankruptcy, change of auditors, departure of directors or officers, change in control, material impairments. Generally due within four business days of the event.Not applicable

Other filings you may see: the annual report to shareholders (the glossy report sent to owners, which contains audited statements), the proxy statement (DEF 14A) for shareholder votes, Form 4 (insider changes in ownership), and Schedule 13D (filed when someone acquires more than 5% of a company's voting stock).

Exam tip: "Annual and audited" = 10-K. "Quarterly and unaudited" = 10-Q. "Sudden material event" = 8-K. Remember "K is for Key annual report; Q is for Quarter; 8 is for the Event."

Audited vs. unaudited statements

An audit is an examination of financial statements by an independent certified public accountant, who issues an opinion on whether the statements fairly present the company's financial position in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP). Possible opinions:

  • Unqualified (clean) – statements fairly present the financial position; the best outcome.
  • Qualified – fairly presented except for a specific issue.
  • Adverse – statements do not fairly present the company's position.
  • Disclaimer – the auditor could not form an opinion.

Unaudited statements (such as those in a 10-Q, or internally prepared statements of a private company) have not had this independent examination, so they carry less assurance. An auditor's opinion is not a guarantee against fraud or a recommendation to invest.

Cash vs. accrual accounting

Under the cash method, revenue is recorded when cash is received and expenses when cash is paid. It is simple and used by many individuals and small businesses. Under the accrual method, revenue is recorded when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands—matching revenues with the expenses that produced them. GAAP requires accrual accounting, so public companies' financial statements are prepared on an accrual basis. This is exactly why the cash flow statement exists: under accrual accounting a company can report a profit while cash is shrinking (for example, if customers haven't yet paid their receivables).

Example: a consulting firm completes a $50,000 project in December but the client pays in February. Under accrual accounting the $50,000 is December revenue (an account receivable); under the cash method it is February revenue.

Trap: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned, not when collected. A question asking why a profitable company might run short of cash is pointing to the accrual/cash difference—look at the cash flow statement.
keyPoints: 10-K = annual report with audited financial statements.
10-Q = quarterly report, unaudited, filed for the first three fiscal quarters.
8-K = current report for material unscheduled events, generally within four business days.
Audits are performed by independent CPAs; an unqualified (clean) opinion is the best result.
Cash method: record when cash is received/paid; accrual method: record when earned/incurred.
GAAP (and therefore public-company reporting) requires the accrual method.
Filings are available on the SEC's EDGAR system.

topics.title: Time Value of Money: PV, FV, NPV, IRR & the Rule of 72
topics.reading:
The core idea

A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future because today's dollar can be invested to earn a return. Time value of money calculations move money forward (compounding) or backward (discounting) in time.

Future value

FV = PV × (1 + r)^n, where r is the rate per period and n the number of periods.

Example: $10,000 invested at 5% compounded annually for 3 years: FV = 10,000 × 1.05^3 = 10,000 × 1.157625 = $11,576.25. More frequent compounding (monthly vs. annually) produces a higher future value at the same stated rate.

Present value

PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n. Discounting tells you what a future amount is worth today.

Example: a client needs $50,000 in 4 years and can earn 6%. PV = 50,000 ÷ 1.06^4 = 50,000 ÷ 1.2625 ≈ $39,605 needed today. The higher the discount rate or the longer the time, the lower the present value.

Discounted cash flow and NPV

A discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis values an investment as the present value of all its expected future cash flows. Net present value compares that value to the cost:

NPV = present value of expected cash inflows − initial investment (cost)

  • Positive NPV – the investment is expected to earn more than the required rate (discount rate); accept.
  • Zero NPV – it earns exactly the required rate.
  • Negative NPV – it earns less than the required rate; reject.

Example: a project costs $100,000 and the present value of its future cash flows, discounted at the firm's 8% required return, is $112,000. NPV = +$12,000, so the project's expected return exceeds 8%.

A bond's price is itself a DCF: the present value of its coupons plus the present value of its par value, discounted at the market rate. When market rates rise, those present values fall—which is why bond prices fall.

Internal rate of return (IRR)

The IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV exactly zero—the rate at which the present value of inflows equals the cost. If IRR is greater than the required return, NPV is positive; if IRR is less than the required return, NPV is negative. For a bond bought at its market price and held to maturity, the IRR is the bond's yield to maturity. IRR assumes cash flows are reinvested at the IRR itself.

Exam tip: Link the pieces: NPV > 0 ⇔ IRR > discount rate. NPV < 0 ⇔ IRR < discount rate. The exam usually tests the relationship, not a full IRR calculation (which requires a financial calculator).

The Rule of 72

A quick estimate of how long it takes money to double at a compound rate:

Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual interest rate (as a whole number), and conversely, rate needed ≈ 72 ÷ years.

Examples: at 8%, money doubles in about 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. At 6%, about 12 years—so $25,000 at 6% grows to roughly $50,000 in 12 years and $100,000 in 24 years. To double in 6 years requires about 72 ÷ 6 = 12%. The Rule of 72 also works for inflation: at 3% inflation, prices double (purchasing power halves) in about 24 years.

Trap: Dividing by the rate in decimal form (72 ÷ 0.08) gives nonsense. Use the whole number. And remember the rule assumes compounding—it doesn't apply to simple interest.
keyPoints: FV = PV × (1 + r)^n; PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n.
Higher discount rate or longer time → lower present value.
NPV = PV of inflows − cost; positive NPV means expected return exceeds the discount (required) rate.
IRR = discount rate that makes NPV equal zero; for a bond held to maturity, IRR = yield to maturity.
NPV > 0 ⇔ IRR > required return; NPV < 0 ⇔ IRR < required return.
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ rate (whole number); rate needed ≈ 72 ÷ years.
A bond's price is the present value of its coupons plus its par value.

topics.title: Descriptive Statistics & Risk-Adjusted Performance
topics.reading:
Measures of central tendency

  • Mean (arithmetic average) – sum of the values ÷ number of values. Sensitive to outliers.
  • Median – the middle value when data are ranked (average of the two middle values for an even count). Not distorted by outliers, so it's preferred for skewed data like incomes or home prices.
  • Mode – the value that occurs most often.
  • Range – highest value minus lowest value; the simplest measure of dispersion.

Example: annual returns of 4%, 6%, 6%, 8% and 16%. Mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8%; median = 6%; mode = 6%; range = 16 − 4 = 12%. The single 16% year pulls the mean above the median.

The geometric mean (compound annual return) is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean and is the better measure of actual multi-period performance.

Standard deviation

Standard deviation measures how widely returns vary around the mean—it is the most common measure of total risk (volatility). In a normal distribution:

  • About 68% of outcomes fall within ±1 standard deviation of the mean.
  • About 95% fall within ±2 standard deviations.
  • About 99.7% fall within ±3 standard deviations.

Example: a fund has a mean return of 10% and a standard deviation of 6%. About two-thirds of the time, returns should fall between 4% and 16%; about 95% of the time, between −2% and 22%. A higher standard deviation means greater volatility.

Correlation

The correlation coefficient ranges from +1 (perfectly positive—assets move together) through 0 (no relationship) to −1 (perfectly negative—move in opposite directions). Diversification reduces risk whenever correlation is less than +1; the lower the correlation, the greater the risk reduction. Combining assets with a correlation of −1 could theoretically eliminate volatility. The coefficient of determination (R-squared) is correlation squared and shows the percentage of a portfolio's movement explained by its benchmark.

Beta

Beta measures a security's volatility relative to the overall market—its systematic risk. The market's beta is 1.0. A beta of 1.3 means the stock tends to move 30% more than the market (up 13% when the market is up 10%); a beta of 0.7 means it tends to move 30% less. Beta is meaningful mainly for well-diversified portfolios, where unsystematic risk has been diversified away.

Alpha and CAPM

The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) gives the return a portfolio should earn for its beta:

Expected return = risk-free rate + beta × (market return − risk-free rate)

Alpha = actual return − expected (CAPM) return. Positive alpha means the manager added value beyond what the portfolio's risk would predict.

Example: risk-free rate 3%, market return 10%, portfolio beta 1.2, actual return 13%. Expected = 3 + 1.2 × (10 − 3) = 3 + 8.4 = 11.4%. Alpha = 13 − 11.4 = +1.6%.

Sharpe ratio

Sharpe ratio = (portfolio return − risk-free rate) ÷ portfolio standard deviation. It measures excess return per unit of total risk; higher is better. Example: a portfolio returned 11% with a standard deviation of 16% while T-bills yielded 3%. Sharpe = (11 − 3) ÷ 16 = 0.50. A second portfolio returning 9% with a 10% standard deviation has a Sharpe of (9 − 3) ÷ 10 = 0.60—better risk-adjusted performance despite the lower raw return. (The Treynor ratio is similar but divides by beta instead of standard deviation.)

Exam tip: Standard deviation and Sharpe use total risk; beta, Treynor and alpha (via CAPM) use systematic risk. Higher Sharpe, higher Treynor and positive alpha are all "good."
Trap: Beta does not measure a stock's total volatility—a stock can have a low beta but high standard deviation if most of its risk is company-specific.
keyPoints: Mean = average; median = middle value (resists outliers); mode = most frequent; range = high − low.
Standard deviation measures total risk/volatility: ~68% within 1 SD, ~95% within 2 SD, ~99.7% within 3 SD.
Correlation runs from −1 to +1; diversification helps whenever correlation < +1.
Beta measures systematic (market) risk; market beta = 1.0.
CAPM expected return = Rf + β(Rm − Rf); alpha = actual − expected.
Sharpe ratio = (Rp − Rf) ÷ standard deviation; higher is better.
Treynor ratio divides excess return by beta instead of standard deviation.

topics.title: Financial & Valuation Ratios
topics.reading:
Liquidity ratios

Liquidity ratios measure a company's ability to pay its short-term obligations.

  • Working capital = current assets − current liabilities (a dollar amount, not a ratio).
  • Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities. A ratio of 2:1 is often cited as healthy for an industrial company.
  • Quick ratio (acid-test) = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities. A stricter test, because inventory may not be quickly convertible to cash. Some texts also remove prepaid expenses.
  • Cash ratio = (cash + marketable securities) ÷ current liabilities—the most conservative.

Example: current assets $800,000 (including $300,000 of inventory); current liabilities $400,000. Working capital = $400,000; current ratio = 800 ÷ 400 = 2.0; quick ratio = (800 − 300) ÷ 400 = 1.25.

Exam tip: The quick ratio is always less than or equal to the current ratio, because it removes inventory from the numerator. Paying off a current liability with cash does not change working capital (both sides fall by the same amount), but it does change the current ratio.

Leverage (solvency) ratios

  • Debt-to-equity ratio = total debt (or total liabilities) ÷ shareholders' equity. Higher values mean more financial leverage and more financial risk.
  • Debt-to-capital (bond ratio) = long-term debt ÷ (long-term debt + equity).
  • Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ interest expense—how many times earnings cover interest; higher is safer for bondholders.

Example: a company has $6 million of debt and $4 million of equity. Debt-to-equity = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5. A company with a high debt-to-equity ratio magnifies returns in good times but is more vulnerable in downturns.

Profitability

Net profit margin = net income ÷ sales. Return on equity (ROE) = net income ÷ shareholders' equity. Return on assets (ROA) = net income ÷ total assets.

Valuation ratios

  • Price-to-earnings (P/E) = market price per share ÷ earnings per share. Growth stocks usually have high P/Es; value stocks low P/Es.
  • Price-to-book = market price per share ÷ book value per share. A low price-to-book is characteristic of value stocks.
  • Dividend yield = annual dividends per share ÷ market price per share. Also called the current yield of a stock.
  • Dividend payout ratio = annual dividends per share ÷ earnings per share. Mature companies and utilities have high payout ratios; growth companies retain earnings and pay little or nothing.
  • Price-to-sales = market price ÷ sales per share (useful when earnings are negative).

Worked example: XYZ trades at $60, earns $4.00 per share and pays quarterly dividends of $0.45. Annual dividend = $1.80. P/E = 60 ÷ 4 = 15. Dividend yield = 1.80 ÷ 60 = 3%. Payout ratio = 1.80 ÷ 4.00 = 45%.

Bond current yield

For bonds, current yield = annual interest ÷ current market price. A 5% coupon bond ($50 per year on $1,000 par) priced at $800 has a current yield of 50 ÷ 800 = 6.25%. Bonds trading at a discount have current yields above the coupon rate; premium bonds have current yields below the coupon rate.

Trap: Always annualize quarterly dividends before computing yield or payout ratio. And don't confuse the payout ratio (dividends ÷ EPS) with the dividend yield (dividends ÷ price).
keyPoints: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; quick ratio removes inventory from current assets.
Working capital = current assets − current liabilities (dollar amount).
Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ shareholders' equity; higher = more leverage and financial risk.
P/E = price ÷ EPS; price-to-book = price ÷ book value per share.
Dividend yield = annual dividends ÷ price; payout ratio = annual dividends ÷ EPS.
Bond current yield = annual interest ÷ market price; discount bond current yield > coupon.
Always annualize quarterly dividends before computing yield or payout ratio.

topics.title: Types of Risk, Capital Structure & Liquidation Priority
topics.reading:
Systematic vs. unsystematic risk

Total risk = systematic risk + unsystematic risk.

Systematic (market, non-diversifiable) risk affects the entire market or economy and cannot be eliminated by diversification. It is measured by beta. Examples:

  • Market risk – the risk that the overall market declines, taking most securities with it.
  • Interest rate risk – rising rates cause bond (and often stock) prices to fall; greatest for long-term, low-coupon bonds.
  • Purchasing power (inflation) risk – inflation erodes the real value of fixed payments; greatest for fixed-income investments like bonds, CDs and fixed annuities.
  • Reinvestment risk – cash flows (coupons, called or maturing principal) must be reinvested at lower rates when rates fall. Zero-coupon bonds have no reinvestment risk before maturity.
  • Exchange-rate (currency) risk and political/geopolitical risk – broad economic or governmental events that move whole markets. (Some texts treat country-specific political and currency risk as partly diversifiable through global diversification.)

Unsystematic (specific, diversifiable) risk affects a single company or industry and can be reduced by diversification. Examples:

  • Business risk – the company's operations fail (poor management, competition, obsolete products).
  • Financial risk – the risk from using debt (leverage); highly leveraged companies may be unable to meet interest payments.
  • Credit/default risk – the issuer fails to pay interest or principal; measured by ratings from agencies such as S&P and Moody's.
  • Liquidity (marketability) risk – an investment cannot be sold quickly at a fair price (limited partnerships, real estate, thinly traded securities).
  • Regulatory/legislative risk – a law or regulation change harms a company or industry.
  • Call risk – a bond is redeemed early, usually when rates have fallen, forcing reinvestment at lower rates.
Exam tip: "Can diversification reduce it?" If yes, it's unsystematic. Owning 50 stocks across industries substantially reduces business and financial risk—but not market, interest rate or purchasing power risk. Only asset allocation, hedging (such as options) or holding cash reduces exposure to systematic risk.

Matching risks to investments: long-term bonds face interest rate and purchasing power risk; Treasury bills face reinvestment and purchasing power risk but essentially no default risk; callable high-coupon bonds face call risk; limited partnerships face liquidity risk; foreign stocks face currency and political risk.

Opportunity cost

Opportunity cost is the return given up by choosing one investment over the next-best alternative. For example, a client who keeps $100,000 in a non-interest-bearing checking account gives up what a money market fund or T-bills would have paid. The risk-free rate (T-bills) is often used as the baseline opportunity cost of any investment.

Capital structure

A company's capital structure (capitalization) is its mix of long-term debt and equity (preferred stock, common stock, paid-in capital and retained earnings). A company heavily financed with debt is highly leveraged: leverage magnifies returns to common shareholders when business is good, but fixed interest payments increase financial risk and the chance of default in bad times. Debt is cheaper for issuers because interest is tax-deductible and creditors take less risk than shareholders.

Liquidation priority

If a corporation is liquidated in bankruptcy, claims are paid in this order:

  1. Secured creditors (e.g., mortgage and equipment trust bondholders), to the extent of their collateral.
  2. Unsecured creditors: priority claims (bankruptcy administrative expenses, certain unpaid wages and taxes) first, then general creditors and debenture holders (senior unsecured).
  3. Subordinated debenture holders.
  4. Preferred stockholders.
  5. Common stockholders—last, with a residual claim.
Trap: Preferred stock is equity, so it ranks behind all debt—including subordinated debentures. Common stock is always last. Debenture holders are unsecured but still ahead of all stockholders.
keyPoints: Systematic (non-diversifiable) risk: market, interest rate, purchasing power (inflation), reinvestment; also broad currency/political risk.
Unsystematic (diversifiable) risk: business, financial, credit/default, liquidity, regulatory, call.
Diversification reduces unsystematic risk only; beta measures systematic risk.
Purchasing power risk is greatest for fixed-income investments; zero-coupon bonds have no reinvestment risk.
Opportunity cost = return forgone on the next-best alternative (often the T-bill rate).
Capital structure = mix of long-term debt and equity; more debt = more leverage and financial risk.
Liquidation order: secured creditors → unsecured creditors/debentures → subordinated debt → preferred stock → common stock.

flashcards.front: Four phases of the business cycle, in order
flashcards.back: Expansion, peak, contraction, trough—then a new expansion (recovery) begins.

flashcards.front: Who controls monetary vs. fiscal policy?
flashcards.back: Monetary: the Federal Reserve (FOMC). Fiscal: Congress and the President, through taxes and government spending.

flashcards.front: Fed buys Treasuries in the open market: effect?
flashcards.back: Bank reserves and the money supply increase; interest rates tend to fall (easy money).

flashcards.front: Discount rate vs. federal funds rate
flashcards.back: Discount rate: what the Fed charges member banks, set directly by the Fed. Fed funds rate: what banks charge each other overnight; the FOMC sets a target.
Percentage of deposits banks must hold rather than lend; the most powerful but least used tool. Lowering it expands the money supply.
Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation rate. Example: 7% nominal with 3% CPI ≈ 4% real.
Normal: long-term yields higher than short-term (upward slope). Inverted: short-term yields higher than long-term; historically signals recession.
Investors demand a premium to lend for longer periods, which explains why the normal yield curve slopes upward.
Growing fear of default and economic weakness (flight to quality into Treasuries). Narrowing spreads signal confidence.

flashcards.front: Who is hurt most by inflation?
flashcards.back: Holders of fixed-income investments and people on fixed incomes. Borrowers and owners of real assets tend to benefit.
U.S. exporters, U.S. multinationals with foreign sales, and U.S. investors holding foreign-currency assets.
U.S. importers, consumers of imported goods, and Americans traveling abroad.

Annual report filed with the SEC, containing audited financial statements, MD&A and risk factors.
Quarterly report for the first three fiscal quarters; financial statements are unaudited.
Current report disclosing a material unscheduled event (merger, bankruptcy, auditor change, officer departure), generally within four business days.
Cash: record revenue/expenses when cash is received/paid. Accrual: record when earned/incurred. GAAP requires accrual.

questions.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence of the phases of the business cycle?
questions.explanation: The economy expands to a peak, contracts to a trough and then recovers into a new expansion. Placing the trough immediately after expansion is the tempting error—an expansion must first reach a peak before activity declines.

questions.q: All of the following are leading economic indicators EXCEPT
choices: building permits for new private housing
questions.explanation: Average duration of unemployment is a lagging indicator—people remain unemployed for a while even after the economy recovers. Building permits, stock prices and new orders all change before the overall economy turns, so they are leading. Don't confuse duration of unemployment with initial jobless claims, which are leading.

questions.q:
Which of the following are coincident economic indicators?
I. Industrial production
II. Nonfarm payroll employment
III. Building permits
IV. The prime rate
questions.explanation: Industrial production and nonfarm payrolls move in step with the economy, confirming the current phase. Building permits are leading (they precede construction), and the prime rate is lagging (banks adjust it after conditions have changed).

questions.q: Gross domestic product (GDP) is best described as
choices: the change in the prices of a basket of consumer goods
the total income earned by a country's citizens anywhere in the world
the difference between a country's exports and imports
the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a period
questions.explanation: GDP measures output produced within a country's borders. Income earned by citizens worldwide describes gross national product/income, the export–import difference is net exports (the trade balance, only one component of GDP), and price changes of a consumer basket describe the CPI.

questions.q: An analyst expecting the economy to enter a recession would most likely recommend overweighting which industry?
questions.explanation: Food and household staples are defensive—people buy necessities regardless of the economy—so their earnings hold up in recessions. Autos, luxury goods and homebuilding are cyclical industries whose sales drop sharply when consumers cut back on big-ticket and discretionary purchases.

questions.q: A country that consistently imports more goods and services than it exports would most likely show
choices: a current account surplus offset by a capital account deficit
a current account deficit offset by a capital (financial) account surplus
a balance of payments that cannot balance
questions.explanation: Imports exceeding exports create a trade deficit, the main part of a current account deficit. Because the balance of payments must balance, the deficit is financed by foreign investment flowing in—a capital/financial account surplus. A trade surplus is the opposite situation.

questions.q: Which of the following tools is used most frequently by the Federal Reserve to implement monetary policy?
questions.explanation: Open market operations—buying and selling government securities—are the Fed's most flexible and frequently used tool. The reserve requirement is the most powerful but least used. Tax rates are fiscal policy, set by Congress and the President, not the Fed.

questions.q: If the Federal Reserve wishes to slow an overheating economy, it would most likely
choices: buy U.S. government securities in the open market
sell U.S. government securities in the open market
questions.explanation: Selling securities drains reserves from the banking system, shrinking the money supply and pushing interest rates up—a tightening move. Buying securities and lowering the discount rate or reserve requirement all ease credit and would stimulate, not slow, the economy.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of fiscal policy?
choices: The Fed purchases Treasury bonds from primary dealers
The FOMC lowers its target for the federal funds rate
Congress passes a bill cutting individual income tax rates
The Fed raises the discount rate
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is government taxation and spending, determined by Congress and the President. The other three choices are monetary policy actions of the Federal Reserve.

questions.q: The interest rate charged by banks to other banks on overnight loans of reserves is the
questions.explanation: The fed funds rate is the overnight interbank lending rate, for which the FOMC sets a target. The discount rate is what the Fed itself charges banks, the prime rate is what banks charge their best corporate customers, and the call loan rate is what banks charge broker-dealers for margin financing.

questions.q: Which of the following interest rates is set directly by the Federal Reserve?
questions.explanation: The Fed directly sets the discount rate charged at its discount window. It sets only a target range for the fed funds rate—the actual rate is determined by banks trading reserves. Commercial banks set the prime rate, and the 10-year Treasury yield is determined by the bond market.

questions.q:
If the Federal Reserve lowers reserve requirements and purchases Treasury securities in the open market, the most likely short-term effects are
I. an increase in the money supply
II. a decrease in the money supply
III. rising prices of outstanding bonds
IV. falling prices of outstanding bonds
questions.explanation: Both actions are expansionary: banks can lend more and the Fed injects reserves, so the money supply rises and interest rates fall. Because bond prices move inversely to interest rates, prices of outstanding bonds rise. Choosing falling bond prices misses the inverse relationship.

questions.q: A client's bond portfolio returned 6.5% last year while the Consumer Price Index rose 2.5%. The client's approximate real rate of return was
questions.explanation: Real return ≈ nominal return − inflation = 6.5% − 2.5% = 4.0%. 6.5% is the nominal return, and 9.0% incorrectly adds inflation instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: An investor in the 24% federal tax bracket holds a CD paying 5% interest during a year when inflation is 3%. The investor's inflation-adjusted, after-tax return is approximately
questions.explanation: After-tax yield = 5% × (1 − 0.24) = 3.8%. Subtract inflation: 3.8% − 3% = 0.8%. The 2.0% answer subtracts inflation but forgets taxes, and 3.8% is the after-tax figure before accounting for inflation.

questions.q: When short-term interest rates are higher than long-term interest rates, the yield curve is
choices: normal, which reflects expectations of steady growth
inverted, which has historically signaled a coming recession
inverted, which signals that inflation is accelerating
flat, which occurs only during deflation
questions.explanation: Short rates above long rates is an inverted (negative) yield curve, which typically follows aggressive Fed tightening and has historically preceded recessions because investors expect rates to fall. A normal curve slopes upward. Inversion reflects expectations of slowing, not accelerating, growth and inflation.

questions.q: The spread between yields on high-yield corporate bonds and U.S. Treasury securities has widened significantly. This most likely indicates
choices: investors expect a strong economic expansion
inflation is expected to decline sharply
investors expect the economy to weaken
questions.explanation: A widening credit spread means investors demand more compensation for default risk—usually because they fear an economic slowdown and flock to the safety of Treasuries. Spreads narrow, not widen, when investors are confident about expansion.

questions.q: Which theory explains the upward slope of a normal yield curve by stating that investors require a premium to tie up their money for longer periods?
questions.explanation: Liquidity preference theory holds that investors prefer shorter maturities and must be paid more to lend long, producing an upward slope. Market segmentation attributes yields to supply and demand within separate maturity segments. The other two are investment theories unrelated to yield curve shape.

questions.q: Which of the following investors is most likely to be harmed by an unexpected rise in inflation?
choices: A homeowner with a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage
A retiree whose income comes from a fixed annuity
An investor holding Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities
questions.explanation: A fixed annuity pays the same dollar amount regardless of prices, so its purchasing power falls as inflation rises. A fixed-rate borrower benefits by repaying with cheaper dollars, TIPS principal is adjusted for inflation, and commodities typically rise with prices.

questions.q: A significant decline in the value of the U.S. dollar relative to foreign currencies would most likely benefit
choices: U.S. companies that export goods overseas
U.S. companies that import foreign goods
Americans planning to travel in Europe
questions.explanation: A weaker dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper for foreign buyers, helping exporters. Importers, American tourists abroad and consumers of imported products all need more dollars to buy the same foreign goods and services, so they are hurt.

questions.q: A U.S. investor bought shares of a Japanese company. Over the year the shares rose 6% in yen, and the yen fell 4% against the U.S. dollar. The investor's approximate return in dollars was
questions.explanation: The dollar return is roughly the local return plus the currency change: 6% + (−4%) = 2%. The yen's decline means each yen converts into fewer dollars, cutting the gain. The 10% answer mistakenly treats the yen's fall as a gain for the U.S. investor.

questions.q: An investor who purchases American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) is subject to which of the following?
choices: Currency risk only if the ADR is sponsored
No currency risk, because ADRs are denominated in U.S. dollars
Currency risk, even though ADRs trade in U.S. dollars
Currency risk only when dividends are declared
questions.explanation: Although ADRs trade and pay dividends in dollars, the underlying foreign shares are valued in their home currency, so exchange-rate changes affect the ADR's dollar price. Dollar denomination does not eliminate currency risk, and sponsorship has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: If U.S. interest rates rise significantly relative to rates in other developed countries, the most likely effect on the U.S. dollar is that it will
choices: strengthen, as foreign investors buy dollar-denominated assets
weaken, as U.S. investors move money abroad
remain unchanged, because exchange rates are fixed
weaken, because higher rates signal inflation
questions.explanation: Higher relative U.S. yields attract foreign capital into U.S. bonds and deposits, increasing demand for dollars and strengthening the currency. Major currencies float, so exchange rates are not fixed.

questions.q: Which of the following sovereign bonds would generally carry the greatest default risk?
choices: A German government bond denominated in euros
An emerging-market government's bond denominated in its own currency
An emerging-market government's bond denominated in U.S. dollars
questions.explanation: A government that borrows in a foreign currency cannot print that currency to repay, and if its own currency collapses the debt becomes much harder to service. An emerging-market government can at least tax and create its own currency to pay local-currency debt, and U.S. and German government bonds carry very low default risk.

questions.q: The risk that a foreign government will nationalize (expropriate) private businesses operating in its country is an example of
questions.explanation: Expropriation, instability, sanctions and other government actions that harm investments are political (geopolitical) risk, which is greatest in emerging markets. Reinvestment, call and purchasing power risks relate to interest rates and inflation, not government seizure.

questions.q: Which financial statement shows a company's financial position at a single point in time?
choices: Statement of retained earnings for the year
questions.explanation: The balance sheet is a snapshot of assets, liabilities and equity as of a specific date. The income statement, cash flow statement and statement of retained earnings all cover a period of time.

questions.q: ABC Corp. reports net income of $12 million, pays $2 million in preferred dividends and has 5 million common shares outstanding. ABC's earnings per share is
questions.explanation: EPS = (net income − preferred dividends) ÷ common shares = ($12M − $2M) ÷ 5M = $2.00. $2.40 forgets to subtract preferred dividends, which belong to preferred holders, not common shareholders.

questions.q:
Which of the following would appear in the financing activities section of a company's statement of cash flows?
I. Payment of cash dividends
II. Purchase of new manufacturing equipment
III. Proceeds from a new bond issue
IV. Depreciation expense
questions.explanation: Financing activities include transactions with the company's owners and lenders: paying dividends and issuing or repaying debt or stock. Buying equipment is an investing activity, and depreciation is a non-cash expense added back in operating activities.

questions.q: Why is depreciation added back to net income when calculating cash flow from operations?
choices: It represents cash set aside to replace equipment
It is paid to creditors after taxes
It is a non-cash expense that reduced reported earnings
questions.explanation: Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life; it lowers net income (and taxes) but no cash leaves the company in that period, so it is added back. It is not a cash reserve for replacement, and it has nothing to do with financing.

questions.q: A company's balance sheet shows total assets of $50 million and total liabilities of $32 million. Its shareholders' equity is
questions.explanation: Assets = liabilities + equity, so equity = $50M − $32M = $18M. Adding assets and liabilities ($82M) has no meaning on a balance sheet.

questions.q:
Which of the following statements regarding a corporation's income statement are TRUE?
I. Interest on bonds is paid from pretax income
II. Dividends on preferred stock are paid from pretax income
III. Common dividends are paid from after-tax income
IV. The income statement reports results as of a single date
questions.explanation: Bond interest is a tax-deductible expense subtracted before taxes, while all dividends—preferred and common—are paid from after-tax net income. The income statement covers a period of time, not a single date; that describes the balance sheet.

questions.q: Which SEC filing contains a public company's audited annual financial statements?
questions.explanation: The 10-K is the annual report and includes financial statements audited by an independent accountant. The 10-Q is quarterly and unaudited, the 8-K reports material events, and Form 4 reports insider ownership changes.

questions.q: A publicly traded company's chief executive officer unexpectedly resigns. The company would disclose this event on Form
questions.explanation: An 8-K current report discloses material unscheduled events such as officer departures, generally within four business days. Waiting for the next 10-Q or 10-K would be too late, and an S-1 is a registration statement for new securities offerings.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Form 10-Q is TRUE?
choices: It is filed within four business days of a material event
It is filed for all four fiscal quarters and is audited
It is filed for each of the first three fiscal quarters and its financial statements are unaudited
It replaces the annual report in years when the company has a loss
questions.explanation: Companies file a 10-Q for the first three quarters only—the fourth quarter is covered by the 10-K—and 10-Q financial statements are reviewed but not audited. The four-business-day deadline applies to the 8-K.

questions.q: A software firm finishes a $40,000 consulting project in November and bills the client, who pays in January of the next year. Under the accrual method of accounting, the revenue is recorded
choices: in November, when it is earned
in January, when the cash is received
half in November and half in January
only after an auditor approves it
questions.explanation: Accrual accounting records revenue when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of cash timing, so the revenue belongs to November (as an account receivable until paid). Recording it in January is the cash method.

questions.q: Financial statements prepared by public companies in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) use
choices: the cash method for revenue and the accrual method for expenses
either method, at the company's option each year
questions.explanation: GAAP requires the accrual method so that revenues are matched with the expenses that produced them. The cash method is common for individuals and small businesses but not permitted for GAAP financial statements.

questions.q: An auditor states that a company's financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, its financial position in accordance with GAAP. This is
questions.explanation: An unqualified opinion is the best outcome: the statements are fairly presented. A qualified opinion adds an "except for" exception, an adverse opinion says the statements are not fairly presented, and a disclaimer means the auditor could not form an opinion.

questions.q: Using the Rule of 72, approximately how long will it take an investment earning 8% compounded annually to double?
questions.explanation: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ 8 = 9. The 12-year answer would apply at a 6% rate, and 7.2 years would require a 10% rate.

questions.q: A client invests $25,000 today in an account expected to earn 6% compounded annually. Using the Rule of 72, approximately what will the account be worth in 24 years?
questions.explanation: At 6%, money doubles about every 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. In 24 years it doubles twice: $25,000 → $50,000 → $100,000. $50,000 reflects only one doubling, and $61,000 reflects simple interest (6% × 24 years = 144% gain), not compounding.

questions.q: A company is considering a project that costs $500,000. Discounted at the company's 10% required rate of return, the present value of the project's expected cash flows is $460,000. Which statement is correct?
choices: The NPV is positive, and the project's IRR is greater than 10%
The NPV is negative, and the project's IRR is less than 10%
The NPV is negative, and the project's IRR is greater than 10%
The NPV is zero, and the project's IRR equals 10%
questions.explanation: NPV = $460,000 − $500,000 = −$40,000. A negative NPV means the project is expected to earn less than the discount rate, so its IRR must be below 10%. NPV and IRR always agree on this: IRR above the required rate would produce a positive NPV.

questions.q: The internal rate of return (IRR) of an investment is the discount rate at which
choices: the investment's cash flows are reinvested at the risk-free rate
the net present value is maximized
the future value equals twice the present value
the net present value equals zero
questions.explanation: By definition, IRR is the discount rate that makes the present value of inflows equal to the cost, so NPV = 0. The Rule of 72 relates to doubling, and IRR actually assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself, not the risk-free rate.

questions.q: A client will need $30,000 in 5 years. All else being equal, which of the following would REDUCE the amount the client must invest today?
choices: A lower assumed rate of return
A higher assumed rate of return
questions.explanation: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n. A higher rate increases the denominator, so less is needed today. A lower rate, a shorter horizon or less frequent compounding all mean the money grows less, so the client must invest more up front.

questions.q: An investor deposits $10,000 in an account earning 5% compounded annually. What will the account be worth at the end of 3 years?
questions.explanation: FV = 10,000 × 1.05^3 = 10,000 × 1.157625 = $11,576.25. $11,500 is simple interest (5% × 3 years), which ignores interest earned on interest. $11,025 is the value after only 2 years.

questions.q: A portfolio has an average annual return of 9% and a standard deviation of 5%. Assuming a normal distribution, approximately 95% of the time the portfolio's annual return should fall between
questions.explanation: About 95% of outcomes fall within ±2 standard deviations: 9% ± 10% = −1% to 19%. The range 4% to 14% is ±1 SD (about 68% of outcomes), and −6% to 24% is ±3 SD (about 99.7%).

questions.q: A portfolio returned 12% last year with a standard deviation of 15%. The risk-free rate was 3%. What is the portfolio's Sharpe ratio?
questions.explanation: Sharpe = (Rp − Rf) ÷ σ = (12% − 3%) ÷ 15% = 0.60. Forgetting to subtract the risk-free rate gives 12 ÷ 15 = 0.80, the tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A portfolio with a beta of 1.2 earned 14% last year. The market returned 10% and the risk-free rate was 2%. Using the capital asset pricing model, the portfolio's alpha was
questions.explanation: Expected (CAPM) return = 2% + 1.2 × (10% − 2%) = 2% + 9.6% = 11.6%. Alpha = 14% − 11.6% = +2.4%. The +4.0% answer simply compares the portfolio to the market, ignoring the portfolio's higher beta.

questions.q: A stock has a beta of 0.8. If the overall market rises 10%, the stock would be expected to
questions.explanation: Beta measures volatility relative to the market: 0.8 × 10% = 8%. A positive beta moves in the same direction as the market, so a decline is incorrect, and 12.5% would require dividing by the beta rather than multiplying.

questions.q:
Five annual returns for a fund were 3%, 5%, 5%, 7% and 20%. Which of the following statements are TRUE?
I. The mean return is 8%
II. The median return is 5%
III. The mode is 7%
IV. The range is 20%
questions.explanation: Mean = 40 ÷ 5 = 8%. Median (middle ranked value) = 5%. Mode (most frequent) = 5%, not 7%. Range = 20% − 3% = 17%, not 20%. The outlier (20%) pulls the mean above the median.

questions.q: An investor wants to reduce portfolio volatility through diversification. Adding an asset with which correlation to the existing portfolio would provide the GREATEST risk reduction?
questions.explanation: The lower the correlation, the greater the diversification benefit; negatively correlated assets tend to move in opposite directions and offset each other. A correlation of +1.0 provides no diversification benefit at all.

questions.q: A company has current assets of $900,000, including inventory of $300,000, and current liabilities of $400,000. Its current ratio and quick ratio are, respectively,
questions.explanation: Current ratio = 900,000 ÷ 400,000 = 2.25. Quick ratio = (900,000 − 300,000) ÷ 400,000 = 1.5. The quick ratio can never exceed the current ratio because it removes inventory from the numerator, which rules out the reversed pair.

questions.q:
XYZ stock trades at $80 per share, earnings per share are $5.00, and the company pays a quarterly dividend of $0.60. Which of the following are correct?
I. The P/E ratio is 16
II. The dividend yield is 3%
III. The dividend payout ratio is 48%
IV. The dividend yield is 0.75%
questions.explanation: Annual dividend = $0.60 × 4 = $2.40. P/E = 80 ÷ 5 = 16. Dividend yield = 2.40 ÷ 80 = 3%. Payout ratio = 2.40 ÷ 5.00 = 48%. The 0.75% yield uses only one quarterly dividend—always annualize first.

questions.q: A corporate bond with a 6% coupon is trading at $960. Its current yield is approximately
questions.explanation: Current yield = annual interest ÷ market price = $60 ÷ $960 = 6.25%. Because the bond trades at a discount, its current yield is above the 6% coupon rate.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best measure of a company's financial leverage?
questions.explanation: Debt-to-equity compares borrowed capital to owners' capital; the higher it is, the more leveraged the company. The quick ratio measures short-term liquidity, the payout ratio measures the share of earnings paid as dividends, and price-to-book is a valuation ratio.

questions.q: A company uses $50,000 of cash to pay off $50,000 of accounts payable. Before the payment, current assets were $300,000 and current liabilities were $150,000. What is the effect of the payment?
choices: Both working capital and the current ratio decrease
Working capital decreases and the current ratio is unchanged
Working capital is unchanged and the current ratio decreases
Working capital is unchanged and the current ratio increases
questions.explanation: Before: working capital $150,000, current ratio 2.0. After: current assets $250,000, current liabilities $100,000—working capital still $150,000, but the current ratio rises to 2.5. Equal reductions on both sides leave the difference unchanged but increase a ratio that is above 1.

questions.q: The dividend payout ratio is calculated as
choices: annual dividends per share ÷ market price per share
annual dividends per share ÷ earnings per share
earnings per share ÷ market price per share
market price per share ÷ book value per share
questions.explanation: Payout ratio = dividends ÷ EPS, showing what fraction of earnings is paid out. Dividends ÷ price is the dividend yield, EPS ÷ price is the earnings yield (the inverse of P/E), and price ÷ book is the price-to-book ratio.

questions.q: Which of the following risks CANNOT be reduced through diversification?
questions.explanation: Market risk is systematic—it affects virtually all securities—so owning more securities does not remove it. Business, financial and credit risk are specific to individual issuers and can be reduced by diversifying across many companies.

questions.q:
Which of the following are considered unsystematic risks?
I. Business risk
II. Purchasing power risk
III. Liquidity risk
IV. Interest rate risk
questions.explanation: Business risk and liquidity risk relate to a particular company or security and can be diversified away. Purchasing power (inflation) risk and interest rate risk affect the entire market and are systematic.

questions.q: In the liquidation of a bankrupt corporation, which of the following would be paid LAST among these claimants?
questions.explanation: The order is secured creditors (mortgage bondholders), then unsecured creditors and debenture holders, then subordinated debt, then preferred stock, then common stock. Because common stock is not listed, preferred stockholders come last among these—equity ranks behind all debt, even subordinated debt.

questions.q: A retired client has invested her entire savings in long-term U.S. Treasury bonds. Which risk is she LEAST exposed to?
questions.explanation: Treasuries are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government, so default risk is minimal. Long-term bonds are highly exposed to interest rate risk and inflation (purchasing power) risk, and coupon payments face reinvestment risk if rates fall.

questions.q: A client keeps $200,000 in a non-interest-bearing checking account for several years. The interest the client could have earned in Treasury bills is best described as
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the return given up by not choosing the next-best alternative; the T-bill rate is the classic benchmark. Liquidity risk is the inability to sell quickly at a fair price—a checking account is perfectly liquid.

questions.q:
An investor holds a high-coupon callable corporate bond. Interest rates have fallen sharply since issuance. The investor faces which risks?
I. Call risk
II. Reinvestment risk
III. Liquidity risk because the bond cannot be sold
IV. The risk that the issuer will increase the coupon
questions.explanation: When rates fall, the issuer is likely to call a high-coupon bond and refinance more cheaply (call risk), leaving the investor to reinvest the principal at lower rates (reinvestment risk). A callable bond can still be sold in the market, and a higher coupon would benefit—not harm—the investor.
